title: E/Z isomerism
keyIdea: A C=C bond cannot rotate, because turning it would break the π bond. So when each carbon of the C=C carries two different groups, the groups are locked into two arrangements: E/Z isomers. Rank the two groups on each carbon by the atomic number of the atom joined to the C=C (on a tie, compare the next atoms). If the two higher-priority groups are on the same side it is Z; if they are on opposite sides it is E.

kid: A single C–C bond lets each end spin, like a wheel on an axle. A C=C double bond is different. Its second bond, the π bond, comes from p orbitals that overlap side by side, above and below the bond. Twist one end and that overlap breaks. That costs about 270 kJ/mol, far more than the molecule gets from heat at room temperature. So a C=C is locked.

Look at but-2-ene. Each carbon of the C=C has a CH₃ and an H. The two CH₃ groups can sit on the same side or on opposite sides. These are two real compounds with the same bonds but a different shape in space. One boils at 4 °C and the other at 1 °C. We call them E/Z isomers.
There is a test. Each carbon of the C=C must have two different groups. But-1-ene has two H atoms on its end carbon. Swap them and you get the same molecule, so it has no E/Z pair.

To name the pair, rank the two groups on each carbon. The atom joined to the C=C with the higher atomic number wins, so Br beats Cl, and Cl beats C. If the first atoms tie, compare the atoms one step further out. Winners on the same side give Z, from the German zusammen, together. Winners on opposite sides give E, from entgegen, opposite.
adult: E/Z isomers have the same atoms joined in the same order, but a different shape in space. They exist because the π bond in C=C, made by p orbitals that overlap side by side, stops the bond from turning. Each carbon of the C=C must also carry two different groups.

In the lab, learners twist a C=C and watch it spring back while a C–C spins freely. They swap groups to make both but-2-enes, find that but-1-ene has no pair, rank groups by priority (atomic number first, then the next atoms on a tie), and fix a cis-means-Z slip.

A common mistake is to rank groups by size or mass, so that CH₃ is thought to beat Cl. Only the atomic number of the atom joined to the C=C counts. Another is to think cis is always Z. In 2-bromobut-2-ene the two CH₃ groups can sit on the same side while Br and the other CH₃ are the priority pair, which makes it E. Students also forget to check both carbons, not just one.
Exam questions often ask learners to draw and label both isomers of but-2-ene, explain with the π bond why the C=C cannot turn, or decide whether a named alkene can show E/Z isomerism.

familyTip: Hold a pencil between two fingers and spin it: that is a single bond. Now hold it with two pencils taped side by side: it will not spin without tearing the tape, like the π bond in C=C.

practice.prompt: Why can a C=C bond not rotate at room temperature?
choices: Turning it would break the sideways overlap of p orbitals that forms the π bond
The two carbon atoms are too heavy to turn
Double bonds are shorter, so the atoms bump into each other
practice.hint: Think about where the second bond of C=C comes from and what it needs.
practice.explain: The π bond is the side-by-side overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond. Rotation pulls them apart, which would need about 270 kJ/mol.

practice.prompt: In a straight chain of {n} carbon atoms, which alkene can show E/Z isomerism?
choices: C=C between carbons 2 and 3 of the {n}-carbon chain
C=C between carbons 1 and 2 of the {n}-carbon chain
Neither: a C=C can always rotate
practice.hint: Check both carbons of the C=C. Does each carry two different groups?
practice.explain: With the C=C at carbon 1, the end carbon carries two H atoms, so there is no E/Z pair. With the C=C at carbon 2 in a chain of {n}, each carbon has an H and a carbon group, so it does.

practice.prompt: On one carbon of a C=C, group X joins through an atom of atomic number {a} and group Y joins through an atom of atomic number {=a+d}. Which group has priority?
choices: Y, joined by atomic number {=a+d}
X, joined by atomic number {a}
Neither: they tie
practice.hint: Compare only the atomic numbers of the atoms joined straight to the C=C carbon.
practice.explain: The higher atomic number wins, so Y ({=a+d}) beats X ({a}). Size and mass of the whole group do not count.

practice.prompt: In 2-bromobut-2-ene, CH₃–C(Br)=CH–CH₃, the two CH₃ groups are on the same side. Which isomer is it?
choices: E: Br and the CH₃ on the other carbon are the priority pair, and they are on opposite sides
Z: the two CH₃ groups are on the same side
Neither: it has no E/Z isomers
practice.hint: On the carbon with Br and CH₃, which group wins by atomic number?
practice.explain: Br (35) beats CH₃ (C is 6) on one carbon; CH₃ beats H on the other. If the CH₃ groups share a side, Br is opposite the priority CH₃, so it is E.

practice.prompt: Which compound has no E/Z isomers?
choices: 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CH–CH₃
Pent-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂CH₃
1,2-dichloroethene, ClCH=CHCl
practice.hint: Look for a carbon of the C=C that carries two identical groups.
practice.explain: In 2-methylbut-2-ene one carbon of the C=C carries two CH₃ groups, so swapping them gives the same molecule.

pool.prompt: Which statement about E/Z isomers is correct?
choices: They have the same structural formula but a different arrangement in space
They have different molecular formulas
They turn into each other at room temperature
pool.hint: Are any bonds different, or only the shape in space?
pool.explain: E/Z isomers are stereoisomers: the same atoms bonded in the same order, but locked in different arrangements by the C=C.

pool.prompt: On one carbon of a C=C are a CH₃ group and a CH₂CH₃ group. Which has priority?
choices: CH₂CH₃: at the first point of difference it has (C, H, H) against (H, H, H)
CH₃: it is smaller
They tie, so the alkene has no E/Z isomers
pool.hint: Both join through carbon. Look at the atoms on that carbon.
pool.explain: Both start with C, so compare the next atoms: (C, H, H) beats (H, H, H). CH₂CH₃ wins.

pool.prompt: A carbon of a C=C carries Cl and CH₃. Which has priority?
choices: Cl, atomic number 17
CH₃, because it has more atoms
CH₃, because it is heavier
pool.hint: Compare the atomic numbers of Cl and of the C in CH₃.
pool.explain: Cl (17) beats C (6). The number of atoms in the group does not matter; CH₃ is also lighter than Cl.

pool.prompt: In (Z)-but-2-ene, where are the two CH₃ groups?
choices: On the same side of the C=C
On opposite sides of the C=C
Both on the same carbon
pool.hint: Z comes from zusammen, German for together.
pool.explain: Z means the priority groups, here the CH₃ groups, are on the same side. Z-but-2-ene is also called cis-but-2-ene.

pool.prompt: An alkene has its C=C between carbons {k} and {=k+1} of a straight chain of {n} carbons. Can it show E/Z isomerism?
choices: Yes: each carbon of the C=C has an H and a different carbon chain
No: alkenes never show E/Z isomerism
No: one carbon has two identical groups
pool.hint: Is the C=C at the very end of the chain?
pool.explain: The C=C starts at carbon {k}, not at carbon 1, so each carbon has an H and a chain. Two different groups on each carbon means E/Z isomers.

pool.prompt: One carbon of a C=C carries groups joined through atomic numbers {a} and {b}; the other carries two identical groups. How many E/Z isomers are there?
choices: None: one carbon has two identical groups
Two
Four
pool.hint: Both carbons need two different groups.
pool.explain: Even though the first carbon has two different groups ({a} and {b}), the second has two identical ones, so swapping them changes nothing.

choices: Breaking the π bond, rotating one end, and re-forming it
Spinning the molecule round in space
Nothing: they are the same compound
pool.hint: What stops the two forms from turning into each other?
pool.explain: Only breaking the π bond allows rotation, for example with heat or light energy. Spinning the whole molecule changes nothing about which side each group is on.

pool.prompt: BrClC=CHCl has Br and Cl on one carbon and Cl and H on the other. Br and the lone Cl on the other carbon are on the same side. Which isomer is it?
choices: Z
E
No E/Z isomers
pool.hint: Find the higher-priority group on each carbon, then check their sides.
pool.explain: Br (35) beats Cl (17) on one carbon; Cl (17) beats H (1) on the other. Br and that Cl share a side, so it is Z.

visual.caption: E/Z or not? Check that each carbon of the C=C has two different groups.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: twist a C=C and watch it lock, swap groups to make E and Z, rank groups by atomic number, and build your own alkenes.
